preamble: Harsusi, a Modern South Arabian language of Oman, has a pharyngealized ('backed') voiceless lateral fricative /ɬˤ/ that contrasts with plain /ɬ/: /jeɬˈboːb/ [jiɬ.ˈboːpʼ] 'to climb 3M.SG.IPFV' against /jeɬˤˈboːb/ [jiɬˤ.ˈboːpʼ] 'to chat 3M.SG.IPFV' (Al Balushi 2023: 119). Al Balushi's instrumental study gives the phoneme three allophones: voiceless [ɬˤ] utterance-initially and medially, voiced [ɮˤ] between vowels, and ejective [ɬʼ] utterance-finally (pp. 152, 280). His Rule 15 states the voicing as /ɬˤ/ → [ɮˤ] / V__V, [ɬˤ] elsewhere (p. 120). The voicing comes from assimilation to the surrounding voiced segments and is not intrinsic: the phoneme is predominantly voiceless, it was voiced in only a few medial tokens, and one speaker produced the same word once fully and once partially voiced (pp. 156, 283–284). Wikipedia (Ḥarsusi language) likewise says /ɬˤ/ may frequently be voiced as [ɮˤ] between vowels. The utterance-final ejective [ɬʼ] is not filed as a separate cell, since it would read the cell ɬʼ > ɬˤ (Proto-Semitic to Harsusi) backwards.

languageExamples.context: Between vowels and, medially, between voiced segments, by voicing assimilation (Rule 15: /ɬˤ/ → [ɮˤ] / V__V, [ɬˤ] elsewhere). The voicing is variable: the phoneme is predominantly voiceless, and the same word from one speaker is fully voiced in one token and partially voiced in another

examples.note: Al Balushi (2023: 120), the example given for Rule 15.

After voiced /ʁ/ and before /oː/, with energy in the voicing bar (Al Balushi 2023: 156–157, Figure 4.22). Chapter 6 transcribes the same word [jə.ʁəˈɬˤo̠ːf], fully voiced in one token and partially voiced in another (pp. 283–284). Counter-token: in /jeɬˤeˈhoːk/ [jiɬˤə.ˈħo̠ːkʰ] 'to laugh 3M.SG.IPFV' the fricative stays voiceless between vowels except at the very start (pp. 154, 156).

sources: Al Balushi, H. (2023). The Phonetics and Phonology of Ḥarsūsi: An Instrumental Phonetics Study. PhD thesis, University of Leeds. https://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/35494/
